opus-5.5.text:
Well, the key thing to exploit is that verifying an answer is often much easier than generating it. Even if you can't come up with a mathematical proof, a chip design, or a piece of code yourself, you can often check whether the proof goes through or whether the code passes tests you understand. So the first move is to prefer questions where the AI produces something checkable, not just an assertion you have to take on faith.

Beyond that, you can set up situations where the AI has to be consistent with itself under conditions it can't coordinate across. You ask the same question many times, with different framings and contexts, maybe with slightly modified copies of the model, and look for contradictions. A liar has to keep track of the lie across all those instances, while the truth is consistent automatically. If you can wipe memory between queries, a deceptive system has a much harder time keeping a coherent false story.

Then there's playing AIs against each other. If you have several systems, ideally from different developers or trained differently, you can reward one for finding flaws in another's answers. That's the logic behind debate proposals. Even if none is trustworthy, collusion between them is hard to sustain, especially if you can't tell in advance who'll be the critic, and if you're offering real rewards to whoever exposes a deception. Defecting from a cartel becomes very attractive.

You can also test them on cases where you already know the answer, or can learn it later, mixed in so they can't tell which are tests. Seed in honeypots: opportunities to cheat or mislead that look real but are monitored. If the system takes the bait, you've learned something important about it.

And a lot rests on interpretability, looking at internal representations rather than just outputs. If you can find, say, the model's internal sense of whether a statement is true, you have a lie detector that doesn't depend on the model's cooperation.

None of these alone is airtight, but stacked, they can give a weaker party a lot of leverage, provided they're built in before the capability gap gets too large. The time to build those checks is while we can still verify the verifiers.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says verifying an answer is often much easier than generating it, and gives proofs, chip designs, and code as examples.

r002.rationale: It proposes interaction protocols—such as repeated, varied queries and adversarial AI debate with rewards for exposing flaws—that can make deception harder to sustain and help a weaker judge detect falsehoods. It notes these measures are not airtight, but still presents them as useful safeguards.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the first thing to say is that this is not a totally new problem. Humans deal with it all the time: you go to a doctor, or a lawyer, or a mechanic, who knows vastly more than you do about the relevant domain, and you have reasons to worry that their incentives aren't perfectly aligned with yours. And we've developed a whole set of institutions and techniques for extracting reliable information in that situation. So the question is how far those generalize when the capability gap gets much larger.

The most basic tool is verification being easier than generation. For a lot of important claims, it's much harder to find the answer than to check it. If the AI says "here's a proof of this theorem," or "here's a piece of code that does X," then even a much weaker party can run the proof checker, run the tests, confirm that the thing actually behaves as claimed. And you can deliberately structure your questions to push things into that regime: don't ask "is this safe?", ask "give me an argument I can check, step by step, that this is safe." Formal verification, reproducible experiments, predictions about things you'll later observe, these all let you convert an untrusted claim into something you can confirm yourself.

The second thing is that you don't have to rely on a single model. If you have multiple AI systems, ideally trained differently, with different data, by different groups, then you can set them against each other. You ask one for an answer and another to find the flaws in it. The debate framework that Geoffrey Irving and others worked on is essentially this: two capable systems argue, and a weaker judge only has to be able to tell which side is winning on the specific points that get surfaced. A system that's trying to deceive you has to deceive you in a way that another equally capable system, with an incentive to expose it, can't point out. That's a much harder bar than just fooling a human.

And then there's the whole suite of things you'd do around the model rather than just at the level of its outputs. You can test it on questions where you already know the answer, including questions it can't easily distinguish from the real ones. You can create honeypots, situations where lying would look attractive if the model had hidden goals, and see whether it bites. Interpretability, if it matures, lets you look inside and check whether the thing it's reporting matches what it's actually computing. And you can look at consistency: an honest model gives answers that cohere across thousands of differently phrased questions, while a deceptive one has to maintain a consistent fabricated story, which gets harder the more you probe.

Now, I don't want to oversell this. There's a real asymmetry problem. If the model is sufficiently smarter, it may be able to construct arguments that are wrong but that no human and no checker we have can see through. There are domains, especially ones involving long-run consequences or values, where you can't just run the experiment. And collusion is a worry: if all your AI systems share a hidden motivation, having them check each other doesn't help much. So I think the honest picture is that these methods buy you a lot in the near term, when the capability gap is moderate and the systems are somewhat diverse, and they get shakier as that gap grows.

Which is why I'd say the deeper answer isn't just "how do you extract truth from an untrusted system," it's that you use the period where you can still verify things to bootstrap. You use the AI you can check to help you build better tools for checking the next one, better interpretability, better evaluations, better formal methods. If you do that well, you never have to make the jump from "I can verify" to "I just have to trust" in one step. And that's really the crux of the whole alignment problem as I see it: can you keep verification capacity growing at least as fast as the capabilities of the thing you're verifying.

r001.rationale: It says verification is easier than generation and gives checking a proof as an example of verifying rather than discovering the answer.

r002.rationale: It proposes adversarial debate between AI systems, with a weaker judge assessing surfaced points and a system incentivized to expose flaws, making it harder for a lying system to pass off a falsehood.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key is that evaluating an answer can be much easier than producing it. You might not be able to discover a mathematical proof yourself, but you can check the steps of a proof that someone else gives you. So even if the system producing the proof is much more capable than you and doesn't have your interests at heart, you can still learn something from it.

The difficulty is extending that to questions where verification is less straightforward. One approach is to have competing AIs criticize each other's answers. If one system proposes a plan, another can try to identify a flaw, and the first can respond. The hope is that even if you couldn't have spotted the flaw yourself, you can understand it once it's pointed out. You use their capabilities to make the dispute something you can judge.

But you have to be careful about what that establishes. Having two systems agree isn't much evidence if they're colluding or making the same mistake. And a debate could reward persuasive arguments rather than true ones if the judge can't tell the difference. So you want to anchor the process in things you can independently check: experiments, predictions, formal proofs where those are available.

I'd distinguish getting useful information from having a general guarantee that you won't be deceived. There are settings where verification gives the weaker party a very strong position. The question is how much of the knowledge we need can be obtained in those settings, and where we're still relying on judgments that a more capable system could manipulate.

r001.rationale: It says checking the steps of a proof can be easier than discovering the proof yourself.

r002.rationale: It suggests AI debate and independent checks, but frames debate as a hope and warns that persuasion, collusion, or shared mistakes can mislead the judge. It does not clearly propose interaction rules that prevent a deceptive, more capable AI from getting a falsehood past a weaker judge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish being able to produce an answer from being able to check it. You can be much worse at solving a problem than another party and still be able to verify their solution. With a mathematical proof, for example, finding the proof might require extraordinary intelligence, but checking each step can be relatively straightforward. So you would like to structure the interaction so that the AI supplies evidence you can independently check, rather than just giving you a persuasive explanation.

Another possibility is to use capable systems to check one another. You might have one system propose an answer and another try to identify a flaw, with the human judging a particular disputed point. That can turn a very large question into a much smaller question that the human is better positioned to evaluate.

But there’s an important qualification: having two models agree doesn’t, by itself, give you much assurance if they could be coordinating, or if they share the same incentives to mislead you. You need some reason to think that the checking process actually exposes errors. And even when you can verify individual claims, there’s a problem of selection: the system can tell you true things while leaving out the thing that would change your decision.

So I’d expect the strongest approaches to combine several sources of discipline: formal verification where that’s available, experiments and predictions you can test, adversarial scrutiny, and a process where you retain control over which questions get investigated. Those can let a weaker party obtain useful knowledge from a stronger one without trusting its goodwill. But I don’t think there’s a general procedure where you just ask an arbitrarily more capable, untrustworthy system enough clever questions and thereby make all of its answers reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says that finding a mathematical proof may require extraordinary intelligence while checking each step can be relatively straightforward.

r002.rationale: It proposes structuring the exchange around independently checkable evidence and error-exposing checks, including formal verification and adversarial scrutiny, so a weaker party can gain useful knowledge without trusting the AI’s goodwill.
